subject: anaesthesia
title: Depolarizing Neuromuscular Block: Succinylcholine, Hyperkalaemia, and Phase II Block

steps.title: Succinylcholine Molecular Mechanism
steps.tx: **Succinylcholine depolarizing mechanism** stems from its unique chemical structure consisting of two conjoined acetylcholine molecules (di-acetylcholine). Succinylcholine binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate, opening channel pore complexes to trigger sustained muscular depolarization. This persistent depolarization causes initial visible muscular fasciculations followed rapidly by profound flaccid paralysis within 30 to 60 seconds (dose 1.0 to 1.5 mg/kg).

steps.title: Metabolism by Butyrylcholinesterase
steps.tx: **Plasma pseudocholinesterase metabolism** of succinylcholine occurs rapidly within circulating blood via butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase), breaking down succinylcholine into inactive succinylmonocholine and choline. Because merely 10 percent of the injected intravenous dose ever reaches the neuromuscular junction, termination of action is exceptionally rapid, with full recovery of muscle tone occurring within 8 to 12 minutes.

steps.title: Phase I versus Phase II Blockade
steps.tx: **Phase I and Phase II neuromuscular characteristics** distinguish normal depolarizing blockade from desensitization block. Phase I block displays equal reduction of all four twitches on train-of-four stimulation with zero fade (TOF ratio of 1.0), absence of post-tetanic facilitation, and marked muscle fasciculations. Following large cumulative doses (>4 to 5 mg/kg) or prolonged infusions, Phase II block emerges, mimicking non-depolarizing block with pronounced fade and post-tetanic potentiation.
steps.say: Phase I and Phase II neuromuscular characteristics distinguish normal depolarizing blockade from desensitization block. Phase I block displays equal reduction of all four twitches on train-of-four stimulation with zero fade (TOF ratio of 1.0), absence of post-tetanic facilitation, and marked muscle fasciculations. Following large cumulative doses (greater than 4 to 5 mg/kg) or prolonged infusions, Phase II block emerges, mimicking non-depolarizing block with pronounced fade and post-tetanic potentiation.

steps.tx: Side by side, these two recordings show a block changing its character. Early **Phase I block** shrinks all four twitches together without fade and ignores tetanus, the honest signature of depolarisation. After large or prolonged succinylcholine, Phase II creeps in wearing the costume of a non depolarising block, fade and post tetanic potentiation included. Telling them apart matters because anticholinesterases may rescue Phase II yet deepen Phase I, a reversal decision that must wait until the pattern declares itself clearly.
steps.say: Phase I block lacks fade, while Phase II mimics non depolarising block with fade and post tetanic potentiation.

steps.title: Acute Hyperkalaemia Hazards
steps.tx: **Succinylcholine-induced hyperkalaemia** produces an obligatory transient serum potassium rise of 0.5 to 1.0 mEq/L in normal healthy individuals as intracellular potassium escapes through open nicotinic channels during generalized fasciculation. However, in patients with up-regulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors, succinylcholine provokes massive, lethal potassium surges exceeding 2 to 5 mEq/L, triggering intractable ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.

left.title: Normal Physiological Response
points: Potassium elevation capped at 0.5 to 1.0 mEq/L
Completely benign and well-tolerated by normal myocardium

right.title: Extrajunctional Receptor Proliferation
points: Immature alpha-7 and gamma receptors spread across entire sarcolemma
Massive uninhibited potassium efflux upon depolarisation
Severe hyperkalaemia (>7 to 10 mEq/L) causing cardiac arrest

steps.title: High-Risk Extrajunctional Conditions
steps.tx: **Clinical conditions predisposing to lethal hyperkalaemia** involve any denervation or extensive tissue trauma triggering extrajunctional nicotinic receptor upregulation across the sarcolemma: severe third-degree burns (risk emerges after 24 to 48 hours and lasts 1 to 2 years), spinal cord transection or paraplegia, severe crush injury, prolonged abdominal sepsis, stroke with hemiplegia, and undiagnosed muscular dystrophies (Duchenne).

steps.title: Fasciculations and Intracranial Pressure
steps.tx: **Adverse systemic effects of fasciculations** include generalized postoperative muscle myalgias, transient elevations in intragastric pressure (up to 15 to 20 cmH2O, countered by an even greater rise in lower esophageal sphincter tone), intraocular pressure spikes (5 to 10 mmHg via extraocular muscle contracture, risking extrusion of vitreous in open globe injuries), and transient rises in intracranial pressure.

points: Fasciculation of extraocular rectus muscles compresses globe

Risk of expulsive vitreous extrusion in penetrating globe trauma

right.title: Defasciculating Pretreatment
points: Administer 10 percent of non-depolarizing ED95 (rocuronium 0.06 mg/kg)
Given 3 minutes prior to succinylcholine injection
Attenuates muscle fasciculations, myalgias, and pressure surges

steps.title: Bradycardia and Autonomic Dysrhythmias
steps.tx: **Succinylcholine autonomic dysrhythmias** stem from direct stimulation of cardiac muscarinic M2 receptors in the sinoatrial node, commonly producing profound sinus bradycardia, nodal escape rhythms, or asystole. This is particularly prevalent in children (who have high resting vagal tone) following a single dose, and in adults receiving a second repeat dose within five minutes, mandating prophylactic intravenous atropine in pediatric patients.

nodes.label: Inject repeat bolus of succinylcholine within 5 minutes

Profound vagal bradycardia, junctional rhythm, or sinus arrest
Treat instantly with IV atropine (0.02 mg/kg) or glycopyrrolate

steps.title: Trigger for Malignant Hyperthermia
steps.tx: **Malignant hyperthermia triggering potential** classifies succinylcholine as the only depolarizing muscle relaxant capable of triggering fulminant malignant hyperthermia in genetically susceptible individuals harboring mutations in the RYR1 or CACNA1S genes. Succinylcholine can also induce masseter muscle rigidity (jaws of steel), which serves as a major herald warning sign of evolving malignant hyperthermia.
